page.h1: HTS Chapter 40: Rubber and Articles Thereof — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: Exporting U.S. Tires & Rubber: Schedule B, Licences, EEI (HTS Ch. 40) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Schedule B codes for tires (4011), gaskets (4016.93) and synthetic rubber, when an export licence is needed (aerospace seals, military tires, Russia), and EEI rules.

intro: A U.S. exporter of tires, synthetic rubber, hoses, belts or rubber seals takes the same five steps as every exporter. Most Chapter 40 goods are **EAR99** and need no export licence, so the extra rules are narrow: a Commerce licence for fluoroelastomer seals made for aircraft (ECCN 1A001.a), for tires, hoses and gaskets specially designed for military aircraft or vehicles when they go to China, Russia or Venezuela (9A610.y, 0A606.y), and for **42 six-digit Chapter 40 codes** shipped to Russia or Belarus, from synthetic rubber and conveyor belts to truck tires and gaskets. Synthetic rubber can also need an EPA **TSCA section 12(b)** export notice, and medical gloves and condoms follow FDA export rules. Shipments to Canada, the largest buyer, need no EEI filing unless a licence is required.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: New tires are classified by the vehicle they are made for: 4011.10 passenger cars (including station wagons and racing cars), 4011.20 buses and trucks, 4011.30 aircraft, 4011.40 motorcycles, 4011.50 bicycles, 4011.70 farm and forestry machines, 4011.80 construction, mining and industrial vehicles (the largest U.S. tire line in 2025, $1.50B) and 4011.90 other, such as light-truck tires. Retreaded and used tires are 4012, gaskets, washers and other seals 4016.93 (the largest single Chapter 40 line, $1.80B), hoses 4009 and conveyor and drive belts 4010. Synthetic rubber in primary forms is 4002, split by polymer (SBR 4002.19, butadiene 4002.20, butyl and halobutyl 4002.31–4002.39, NBR 4002.59, EPDM 4002.70).

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Most tires, synthetic rubber and rubber articles are EAR99. The listed items are: seals, gaskets, sealants and fuel bladders specially designed for aircraft or aerospace use and made more than 50% of fluorinated polyimides or fluorinated phosphazene elastomers (ECCN 1A001.a; the elastomers themselves are 1C009.b and 1C009.c); tires specially designed for military aircraft (9A610.y.1); tires (except run-flat), brake, cooling, hydraulic and pneumatic hoses, and gaskets and O-rings specially designed for military ground vehicles (0A606.y); and spacecraft tires (9A515.y.46). The .y items need a licence only for China, Russia or Venezuela and for embargoed destinations. Tires specially designed for civil aircraft can fall under 9A991.d, which is controlled for anti-terrorism reasons only.

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.
steps.chapterNote: Russia and Belarus: a Commerce licence is required for the 42 six-digit Chapter 40 codes in Supplement No. 4 to 15 CFR Part 746: synthetic rubber (4002.11–4002.99), compounded rubber (4005), camel-back strips (4006.10), non-cellular rubber sheet (4008.21), some hoses (4009.12, 4009.41), all conveyor and transmission belts (4010), bus and truck tires (4011.20), aircraft tires (4011.30), retreaded and used tires (4012) and gaskets and other rubber articles (4016.93, 4016.99). Passenger-car tires (4011.10) and construction and mining tires (4011.80) are not on that list. Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Syria are covered by country-wide rules.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: Shipments to Canada (28% of Chapter 40 exports) need no EEI unless they need a licence or another exception applies (15 CFR 30.36). A truckload of tires or a container of synthetic rubber to Mexico or overseas is almost always over $2,500 per Schedule B number, so file.

rules.title: Fluoroelastomer seals, gaskets, sealants and fuel bladders specially designed for aircraft or aerospace use (ECCN 1A001.a), and fluorinated phosphazene elastomers and fluorinated polyimides (1C009.b–c), need a licence for the destinations the Country Chart marks under national security (NS Column 2)

citations.label: Commerce Control List, ECCN 1A001 and 1C009 (15 CFR 774 Supp. 1)

rules.title: Tires, hoses, gaskets and O-rings specially designed for military aircraft (ECCN 9A610.y.1), military ground vehicles (0A606.y) or spacecraft (9A515.y.46) need a licence for China, Russia or Venezuela and for embargoed destinations

citations.label: Commerce Control List, ECCN 0A606, 9A515 and 9A610 (15 CFR 774 Supp. 1)
15 CFR 742.6(a)(7) (.y items to China, Russia or Venezuela)

rules.title: Russia and Belarus: a licence is required for the 42 six-digit Chapter 40 codes in Supplement No. 4 to Part 746 (synthetic and compounded rubber, belts, bus, truck and aircraft tires, retreaded tires, gaskets and other rubber articles); applications are reviewed under a policy of denial

TSCA section 12(b): notify EPA of the export of a chemical substance or mixture, such as a synthetic rubber or compounded rubber, that is subject to certain EPA data requirements, rules or orders, within seven days of forming the intent to export or on the date of export, whichever is earlier

citations.label: EPA: TSCA requirements for exporting chemicals

rules.title: Medical gloves (patient examination and surgeon's gloves) and condoms are medical devices: devices legally marketed in the U.S. can be exported without FDA permission, and FDA issues Certificates to Foreign Government that many importing countries ask for; devices not cleared in the U.S. may be exported only under FD&C Act section 801(e) or 802, with the records in 21 CFR 1.101

New aircraft tires and other aircraft articles: the maker can obtain an FAA export airworthiness approval, issued on FAA Form 8130-3, which the importing country's aviation authority may require before the part is installed

groups.label: Natural rubber: latex, smoked sheets, TSNR, balata, gutta-percha, chicle
Synthetic rubber: SBR, butadiene, butyl, chloroprene, NBR, EPDM, isoprene
groups.note: Synthetic rubbers are chemical substances under TSCA; check the polymer against EPA's list of chemicals subject to export notification. Fluorinated phosphazene elastomers (1C009.c) are the only listed elastomer; ordinary fluoroelastomers (FKM), EPDM, SBR, butyl and NBR are EAR99. Every 4002 subheading is on the Russia and Belarus list.

groups.label: Rubber waste, scrap, powder and crumb
groups.note: No U.S. export permit is needed for rubber scrap and crumb, but many buyers restrict waste imports; check the destination first.

groups.label: Compounded rubber, unvulcanized (masterbatch, solutions, sheets)
groups.note: Compounded rubber is a mixture under TSCA, so the 12(b) notice applies when it contains a chemical subject to an EPA action.

groups.label: Other unvulcanized forms: camel-back retread strips, rods, tubes, discs
groups.note: Only camel-back strips for retreading (4006.10) are on the Russia and Belarus list.

groups.label: Plates, sheets, strip, rods and profiles of vulcanized rubber, incl. foam
groups.note: Only non-cellular rubber plates, sheets and strip (4008.21) are on the Russia and Belarus list.

groups.label: Tubes, pipes and hoses, incl. brake hoses
groups.note: Brake, cooling, hydraulic and pneumatic hoses specially designed for military ground vehicles are 0A606.y; commercial hoses are EAR99. Only 4009.12 and 4009.41 are on the Russia and Belarus list.

groups.label: Conveyor belts and transmission belts (V-belts, timing belts)
groups.note: Every conveyor and transmission belt subheading is on the Russia and Belarus list.

groups.label: New pneumatic tires: car, light truck, truck and bus, OTR, farm, aircraft, motorcycle, bicycle
groups.note: Car, truck, farm and mining tires are EAR99. Tires specially designed for military aircraft (9A610.y.1) or military ground vehicles (0A606.y.15) need a licence for China, Russia or Venezuela. Bus and truck tires (4011.20) and aircraft tires (4011.30) are on the Russia and Belarus list; car and mining tires are not.

groups.label: Retreaded and used tires, solid tires, tire treads and flaps
groups.note: Retreaded aircraft tires (4012.13) can carry an FAA Form 8130-3 like new ones. All retreaded, used and solid tires are on the Russia and Belarus list.

groups.label: Hygienic and pharmaceutical articles: condoms, nursing nipples
groups.note: Condoms are FDA-regulated medical devices (21 CFR 884.5300).

groups.label: Rubber gloves and apparel: medical, surgical, nitrile and latex gloves, aprons
groups.note: Medical examination and surgeon's gloves are FDA-regulated medical devices; industrial and household gloves are not.

groups.label: Other articles of vulcanized rubber: gaskets, seals, O-rings, mats, bands, anti-vibration parts
groups.note: Fluoroelastomer seals made for aircraft or aerospace use can be 1A001.a, and gaskets and O-rings specially designed for military ground vehicles are 0A606.y.9; standard automotive and industrial gaskets are EAR99. Gaskets (4016.93) and other rubber articles (4016.99) are on the Russia and Belarus list.

groups.label: Hard rubber (ebonite) and articles of hard rubber

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

savings.title: Meet the USMCA rule of origin for tires and rubber parts
savings.saves: Mexico's general rate on non-qualifying goods (35% on car and farm tires and 25–35% on truck tires since January 1, 2026, and 25% on gaskets of tariff item 4016.93.04) and Canada's MFN rate (7% on car and truck tires).
savings.appliesTo: New tires and belts (40.10–40.11) qualify when made from materials of any heading other than 40.09–40.17, so a tire built in a U.S. plant from imported natural rubber, synthetic rubber, compounded rubber, carbon black, cord and steel bead wire qualifies. Gaskets and other rubber articles of 4016.10–4016.95 qualify when made from materials of another heading, and synthetic rubber (4001.10–4002.99) when made from another subheading.
savings.document: A USMCA certification of origin with the nine data elements in Annex 5-A, backed by bills of material showing where the inputs are classified.
savings.caveat: Tires, hoses, belts, gaskets and vibration-control parts sold for use in vehicles are also covered by the USMCA automotive appendix, which can add a regional value content test; check Annex 4-B and its Appendix. Keep the records for at least five years.

savings.title: Ask the Chinese buyer to apply for a tariff exclusion
savings.saves: China's 2018–2019 counter-tariffs on the goods covered: 5% on car and truck tires, 25% plus 2.5% on most construction and mining tires, 10% on gaskets and 5–25% on synthetic rubber. The 10% extra duty, China's normal rate and any anti-dumping duty still apply.
savings.appliesTo: U.S. goods on China's counter-tariff lists bought by a Chinese company under the Tariff Commission's market-based exclusion process. Exclusions are valid until December 31, 2026 under the November 2025 U.S.–China deal.
savings.document: An application by the Chinese importer to China's State Council Tariff Commission. Once approved, the exclusion covers only that importer's purchases from the U.S., up to the approved amount.
savings.caveat: Only the Chinese buyer can apply. No extension past December 31, 2026 has been announced (see Tariff updates).

citations.label: Tariff Commission Announcement No. 2 of 2020 (exclusion process)
White House fact sheet on the U.S.–China deal, Nov 1, 2025

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
